On October 19, 2010, Executive Order 13555 established the White House Initiative on Educational Excellence for Hispanics within the Department of Education. It superseded the White House Initiative on Educational Excellence for Hispanic Americans, which had been established by Executive Order 13230 of October 12, 2001. This Initiative was housed within the Department’s White House Initiative on Educational Excellence for Hispanics Staff, which was led by an Executive Director appointed by the Secretary of Education. The Initiative was advised by the President's Advisory Commission on Educational Excellence for Hispanics and supported by the Interagency Working Group, both established by the Executive Order.

The mission of the Initiative was to help restore the United States to its role as the global leader in education and to strengthen the Nation by expanding educational opportunities and improving educational outcomes for Hispanics of all ages and by helping to ensure that all Hispanics receive a complete and competitive education that prepares them for college, a career, and productive and satisfying lives. The Staff worked to expand educational opportunities, improve education outcomes, and deliver a complete and competitive education for all Hispanics.

Consistent with the law, the Staff was to promote, encourage, and undertake efforts designed to meet the following objectives: increasing general understanding of the causes of the educational challenges faced by Hispanic students; increasing the percentage of Hispanic children who entered kindergarten ready for success by improving access by Hispanics to high-quality programs and services that encouraged the early learning and development of children from birth through age 5; and implementing innovative education reform strategies and practices in America's public schools to ensure that Hispanic students, like their peers, received a rigorous and well-rounded education, and had access to student support services that prepared them for college, a career, and civic participation. Furthermore, it was to ensure that all Hispanic students had access to excellent teachers and school leaders, in part by supporting efforts to improve the recruitment, preparation, development, and retention of successful Hispanic teachers and school leaders and other effective teachers and school leaders responsible for the education of Hispanic students. The Staff was responsible for reducing the dropout rate of Hispanic students and helping Hispanic students graduate from high school to prepare for college and a career, in part by promoting a positive school climate and supporting successful and innovative dropout prevention and recovery strategies that better engaged Hispanic youths in their learning, help them catch up academically, and provide those who had left the educational system with pathways to reentry. It was to increase college access and success for Hispanic students and provide support to help ensure that a greater percentage of Hispanics completed college and contributed to the goal of having America lead the world in the proportion of college graduates by 2020, in part through strategies to strengthen the capacity of Hispanic-Serving Institutions, community colleges, and other institutions of higher education serving large numbers of Hispanic students. Additionally, it was to enhance the educational and life opportunities of Hispanics by fostering positive family and community engagement, improving the quality of, and expanding access to, adult education, literacy, and career and technical education, as well as increasing opportunities for education and career advancement in the fields of science, technology, engineering, and mathematics. 

In working to fulfill its mission and objectives, the Staff helped ensure that Federal programs and initiatives administered by the Department and other agencies were serving and meeting the needs of Hispanic children, youths, and adults; worked closely with the Executive Office of the President on key Administration priorities related to the education of Hispanics; and increased the Hispanic community's participation in, and capacity to participate in, the Department's programs and education-related programs at other executive departments and agencies. It also advised Department officials and, through the Interagency Working Group, other agency officials on issues related to the Hispanic community and the educational attainment of Hispanic students; and advised the Secretary on the development, implementation, and coordination of educational programs and initiatives at the Department and other agencies designed to improve educational opportunities and outcomes for Hispanics of all ages. The Staff also encouraged and developed partnerships with public, private, philanthropic, and nonprofit stakeholders to improve Hispanics' readiness for school, college, and career, as well as their college persistence and completion; and developed a national network of individuals, organizations, and communities to share and implement best practices related to the education of Hispanics. The Staff worked with the other White House Initiatives on Historically Black Colleges and Universities, Tribal Colleges and Universities, and Asian-American and Pacific Islanders whenever appropriate. The Secretary and the Executive Director of the Initiative, in consultation with the Interagency Working Group and the Chair of the Commission, developed and submitted to the President recommendations designed to advance and promote educational opportunities and attainment for Hispanics, including recommendations for short- and long-term initiatives.

On July 9, 2020, Executive Order 13935 superseded the White House Initiative on Educational Excellence for Hispanics with the new White House Hispanic Prosperity Initiative.

The Fourth Service Command was established by War Department General Order 35, July 22, 1942, replacing the IV Corps Area. Headquartered in Atlanta it embraced the States of North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, Florida, Aalabama, Tennessee, and Mississippi.

The Fourth Service Command performed administrative and supply functions for all U.S. Army elements within its geographical limits, including (but not limited to) initial procurement, classification, and assignment of military personnel; command and training of all units directly assigned to it; command of Army Service Forces (ASF) replacement training centers, unit training centers, and schools; supervision, through each installation's commanding officer, of the requisitioning, storage, and issuance of supples and equipment to meet military requirements; repair and salvage activities; supervision of housing and hospitalization of troops; supervision of Special Services activities; ordnance maintenance; provision and operation of laundry facilities; repair and maintenance of real property, operation of utilities; purchase or lease of real estate at installations under its jurisdiction; the rendering of legal, financial, and administrative services; protection of Army installations, plants of Army contractors, and civilian lives and property against subversive activities and casual hazards; and supervision of all ASF intelligence and counter intelligence activities within its jurisdiction.

The Fourth Service Command was abolished on June 11, 1946, as directed by War Department Circular 138 of May 14, 1946, with residual functions devolving upon Seventh Army.

From the earliest days of the Republic, Presidents have designated special diplomatic envoys for specific assignments, primarily overseas. The President appointed the first official specifically to bear the title of Ambassador at Large on March 12, 1949, under the authority vested in Article II, Section 2 of the U.S. Constitution that empowers the President, with the advice and consent of the Senate, to appoint Ambassadors, other public Ministers, and Consuls. Presidents have usually appointed Ambassadors at Large to deal with specific foreign policy issues which have been frequently, but not always, spelled out in their commissions.

Arthur J. Goldberg served as Ambassador at Large and U.S. Representative to the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe from September 23, 1977, through July 27, 1978.

record.administrativeHistoryNote: The Fisheries Section was organized in August 1917 under Kenneth Fowler. Its function was to stimulate the production of fish, to supervise the licensing of salt-water fishermen, to investigate cases of apparent excessive prices, to maintain "fair maximum" prices on frozen fish, and to survey and analyze, in conjunction with the Retail Fish Section of the Wholesale and Retail Division, retail fish margins. The Fisheries Section held conferences concerning markets, supplies, transportation and distribution of fish. In June 1918, a Retail Fish Section was established in the Distribution Division, and to it were transferred matters pertaining to the retail prices of selling fish. It was transferred nominally to the Canned Foods Division in October 1918 but appears to have continued to function as a separate unit.

record.administrativeHistoryNote: The Newport Naval Torpedo Station was established in 1869 on Goat Island in Newport (Rhode Island) Harbor to work on torpedo development, experimentation, and testing.  Work at the Station between 1870 - 1900 was centered on research and testing of mines and spar torpedoes.  Various systems of torpedo propulsion were tested by Station personnel.  The Station also manufactured main charge explosives and explosive components, and staff experimented with shipboard electrical systems.  During the first decade of the twentieth century, the Station began the process of manufacturing torpedoes.  However, during World War I, the Station stopped this work and concentrated on manufacturing mines, depth charges, and aerial bombs, and the facility expanded to accommodate the new activity.  After World War I, the Station returned to manufacturing of torpedoes and the development of the Mark I and Mark II torpedoes.  The 1930s saw activity at the Station focus on torpedo research, development, and manufacturing for use on ships.  Activity increased with the threat of war, and after the entry of the U.S. into World War II, the Station geared up for wartime production of torpedoes and explosive components such as fuzes, igniters, and detonators. When the war ended in 1945, the Station slowed down its production of offensive weapons, and in 1946 the manufacturing program ended and the Station returned to torpedo research, design, experimentation, and storage. From 1946 to 1951, work at the Station on Goat Island diminished, and in December of 1951 the Station was officially disestablished.  Research and development activity was transferred to nearby Coddington Cove under a new command designated as the Naval Underwater Ordnance Station.

record.administrativeHistoryNote:
The U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom, established by the International Religious Freedom Act of 1998 (Publ. L. 105-292), approved October 27, 1998,  was an independent nine-member, bipartisan U.S. Government agency that was created to monitor the status of freedom of thought, conscience, and religion or belief abroad, as defined in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and related international instruments and to give independent policy recommendations to the President, the Secretary of State and the U.S. Congress. The Commission was funded entirely by the Federal Government on an annual basis and staffed by government employees.

The Commission was responsible for determining the effect of other countries' policies on religious groups, and if necessary, holding Congressional hearings to educate Congress and the public about religious persecution around the world. The Commission could not implement sanctions on countries that violated religious freedom as it only had advisory and monitoring authority, including the authority to hold hearings. While the Department of State reports contained detailed country-by-country analyses of religious freedom, the Commission's report covered few countries, but made policy recommendations to the executive and legislative branches of the Government. The Commission report also reviewed and analyzed the work of Department of State.

record.administrativeHistoryNote: The War Resources Council was established in the Department of the Interior by Administrative Order 1636, January 14, 1942, as the sucessor to the Defense Resources Council which the Secretary had established on June 15, 1940. The Council was composed of the Director, the Under Secretary of the Interior, the Commissioner of Reclamation, the Director of the Bureau of Mines, and the Assistant Commissioner of the General Land Office. Its purpose was to advise the Secretary of the Interior regarding the war program for the Department and to coordinate the activities of the bureaus, offices, and services in carrying out this program. On March 9, 1942, the Western War Resources Council (comprising western field representatives of the Department) was organized in Salt Lake City; and branches were organized in Arizona, California, Montana, Nevada, and New Mexico. The War Resources Council was abolished on December 20, 1945.

record.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Procurement Policy Branch, establsiehd in January 1946, formulated and promulgated policies and general procedures governing activities of the Navy with respect to the procurement of material and facilities. It reviewed and evaluated compliance with such policies and procedures, and issued orders as required to assure compliance. Among specific functions of the Branch were the following: assisted the Bureaus in the negotiation of contracts and relations in general and with Navy contractors; reviewed and approved requests for authority to enter into contracts, amendments and redeterminations above the minimum dollar value; prepared analyses for the Secretary on procurement and contract matters and business trends; and allocated procurement responsibility among the Bureau. The Branch also formulated and promulgated policies and procedures with respect to insurance, and performances and payment bonds, and advised on insurance problems. It formulated Navy policies respecting settlement of terminated contracts and related matters of industrial readjustment; and promotes procurement coordination with the Army and Air Force. 

In 1948, the Branch became the Procurement Policy Division, which formulated and promulgated policies and general procedures governing activities of the Navy with respect to the procurement of supplies and services. The Division reviewed and evaluated compliance with such policies and procedures and issued orders as reuired to assure compliance. It also coordinated the procurement activities of the Navy with those of other segments of the National Military Establishment.

record.administrativeHistoryNote: On July 3, 1919, the remaining staff and troops of Third Army, which had been dissolved the day before, was designated American Forces in Germany. Major General Edward F. McGlachlin assumed temporary command, pending the arrival of Major General Henry T. Allen. who had been selected as permanent commander. American Forces in Germany took over the former Third Army area, comprising the North Sector of the Coblenz bridgehead and the area to the west of the Rhine. In January 1923, American Forces in Germany was ordered to terminate its occupation and return to the United States and on January 27, 1923 General Allen turned over command of the American area to French troops. On January 24 the entire American force, except the commanding general and a small number of officers and men who remained to settle up American affairs, entrained for Antwerp, Belgium; leaving that port the following day for New York. Major General Allen left Coblenz on February 19 and sailed from Bremen on February 21 to New York. On April 30, 1923, headquarters at Coblenz was demobilized and on July 11 the five remaining representatives of the American Army, left Germany.

record.administrativeHistoryNote: Regional control was established in the Venezia Region in April 1945 simultaneously with Allied Military Government. Initially, the Venezia Region included the Provinces of Belluno, Bolzano, Padova, Rovigo, Trento, Treviso, Udine, Venezia, Verona, and Vicenza. However, on July 15, 1945, the continuing crisis along the Italian-Yugoslav border necessitated placing Udine and Treviso Provinces and the port of Venezia under the control of Allied Military Government, 13th Corps. In addition, nationality and border issues regarding Bolzano Province forced the western Allies to detach this province from the Venezia Region. By December 1945, both Treviso and Bolzano were restored to control of the Region and Udine was made a separate area of AMG responsibility. Regional control was lifted on December 31, 1945; a small liaison office operated through 1946.

In a commencement address at the U.S. Naval Academy in May 1998, President Bill Clinton announced that the nation would do more to protect its citizens against the growing threat of chemical and biological terrorism. As part of this effort, he said, the Department of Defense would form ten teams to support state and local authorities in the event of an incident involving weapons of mass destruction. These WMD Civil Support Teams were established to deploy rapidly to assist a local incident commander in determining the nature and extent of an attack or incident; provide expert technical advice on WMD response operations; and help identify and support the arrival of follow-on state and Federal military response assets. They were joint-service units and, as such, could consist of both Army National Guard and Air National Guard personnel.

In Fiscal Year 2000, Congress established an additional seventeen civil support teams to expand the nation's capabaility and decrease the response time for WMD incidents.

The 55th Weapons of Mass Destruction Civil Support Team, based at St. Paul, was certified on December 17, 2001.

Section 711 of the John Warner National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2007 (120 Stat.2083; Publ. L. 109-364), approved October 17, 2006, required that the Secretary of Defense establish a task force to examine matters related to the future of military health care. As directed by the Act, in December 2006 the Secretary of Defense appointed fourteen members to the Task Force on the Future of Military Health Care. The Task Force includes individuals from within and outside the Department of Defense, with wide expertise in issues related to health care programs and costs. 

The Task Force addressed ten specific elements relevant to the future of military healthcare and issue a final report with its assessment and recommendations within twelve months. The issues concerned were:

                (A) Wellness initiatives and disease management programs of the Department of Defense, including health risk tracking and the use of rewards for wellness.

                (B) Education programs focused on prevention awareness and patient-initiated health care.

                (C) The ability to account for the true and accurate cost of health care in the military health system.

                (D) Alternative health care initiatives to manage patient behavior and costs, including options and costs and benefits of a universal enrollment system for all TRICARE users.

                (E) The appropriate command and control structure within the Department of Defense and the Armed Forces to manage the military health system.

                (F) The adequacy of the military health care procurement system, including methods to streamline existing procurement activities.

                (G) The appropriate mix of military and civilian personnel to meet future readiness and high-quality health care service requirements.

                (H) The beneficiary and Government cost sharing structure required to sustain military health benefits over the long term.

                (I) Programs focused on managing the health care needs of Medicare-eligible military beneficiaries.

                (J) Efficient and cost effective contracts for health care support and staffing services, including performance-based requirements for health care provider reimbursement.

In addition, the Act required that the Task Force produce an interim report by May 31, 2007 for submission to the Secretary of Defense and the Committees on Armed Services of the Senate and House of Representatives. The interim report was to focus on one of the ten elements, specifically, the "beneficiary and Government cost sharing structure required to sustain military health benefits over the long term, particularly with regard to cost sharing under the pharmacy benefits program."

The Task Force operated as a subcommittee of the Defense Health Board. It held its first meeting on January 16, 2007. Subject to the Federal Advisory Committee Act, as amended, the Task Force conducted a number of public meetings to gather information from interested parties, including the public, on the issues listed in its charge. 

The Task Force officially terminated on June 27, 2008 as required by law.

The Revolutionary Army was disbanded on November 5, 1783, in accordance with proclamation of Congress of October 18, 1783. In the belief that standing armies in time of peace were "inconsistent with the principles of republican governments, dangerous to the liberties of a free people, and generally converted into destructive engines for establishing despotism," the Congress of the Confederation, on May 26, 1784, resolved that western posts should be garrisoned by state militia or by the use of Continental troops then at West Point, New York. To implement this belief, Congress, in its resolution of June 2, 1784, directed that all troops--including all officers above the rank of captain--in the service of the United States be discharged, except 25 privates to guard stores at Fort Pitt and 55 privates to guard stores at West Point and other magazines. Thus Henry Knox, Brigadier General of Artillery, who had served as commander in chief since the resignation of George Washington on December 23, 1783, was honorably discharged, and the position of commander in chief was abolished. Also discharged were all officers of the First American Regiment of Infantry, located at Fort Pitt, under the command of Colonel Henry Jackson.

On June 3, 1784, Congress recommended to the states of New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, and Connecticut, that 700 men be furnished by these states "for securing and protecting the northwestern frontiers of the United States and for garrisoning the posts soon to be evacuated by the troops of his Britannic Majesty. The term of service was to be one year, with the organization comprised of eight companies of infantry and two of artillery. The officers were selected from the several states represented, with Lieutenant Colonel Josiah Harmar of Pennsylvania as commandant. As commander of this single unit, of the Army, Colonel Harbar in effect commanded the Army of the United States. During the succeeding five years, this frontier force was maintained by an annual resolution of Congress; not until 1789 was it legally declared to be "troops in the service, of the United States: given the designation "The Regiment of Infantry." On July 31, 1787 Harmar was breveted brigadier general and placed on duty as general in chief of the Army consisting of less than 600 men. 

With Miami Indian troubles on  the northwest frontier, Congress, in an act of March 3, 1791 (1 Stat. 22), empowered the President of the United States to raise an additional regiment of infantry, which, exclusive of the commissioned officers, and consisting of 912 non commissioned officers, privates and musicians and to provide for further protection of the frontiers. Congress changed the regimental designation of the Regiment of Infantry to the First Regiment of Infantry and added to the Army The Second Regiment of Infantry. In September of that year, both regiments of infantry with some militia, all under command of Governor Arthur St. Clair of the Nrthwest Territory, were again sent against the Miami Indians. Fighting against the Miamis, St. Clair''s Soldiers were untrained, ill equipped, underfed, and sickly. This resulted in a disastrous defeat, suffering a loss in killed and wounded of nearly 900 out of a total strength of 1400.

Upon the resignation of St. Clair on March 5, 1792, Anthony Wayne was appointed major general and succeeded St. Clair as general in chief, under provisions of an act of the same day (1 Stat. 241). By virture of the same act the Army of the United States was designated as the Legion of the United States, effective September 4, 1792.

In 1792, Congress created the Legion of the United States, which was a combined arms force of infantry, cavalry, and artillery under the command of Major General Anthony Wayne. The First Regiment of Infantry became the Infantry of the 1st Sub-Legion.

In the United States title to land derives from a variety of sources depending on the history of the area in which the land is located. In the so-called “public land states” (Alabama, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Florida, Idaho, Illinois, Iowa, Indiana, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, New Mexico, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, South Dakota, Utah, Washington, Wisconsin, and Wyoming) and Alaska, almost all lands are owned either by the Federal Government or by persons deriving their land titles from the Government. (Excepted were those lands granted to individuals from foreign sovereignties prior to cessation of the area to the United States. These were handled as private land claims.) The basic operating unit that effected the transfer of title of a piece of the public domain to private ownership was the district land office.

When from time to time it was decided to open to entry certain portions of the public domain, a land district was created, usually by an act of Congress, and all transactions connected with obtaining titles to land in that area had to be initiated and carried on though the district land office. Until the 1920''s each land district ordinarily had two officials in charge, a Register and a Receiver, who jointly conducted the business of the office. The receiver was primarily responsible for the moneys taken in at the office; the register for the necessary record keeping.

A person wishing to make an “entry” (i.e., to initiate proceedings that if successfully completed would result in the issuance to him of a patent to a tract of land) of any type went before the Register and indicated the tract of land to which he desired to obtain title together with the class of entry he desired to make. The entryman, the Register, and the Receiver then filled out and signed a series of documents. In the early period these ranged from the simple applications to purchase and receipts executed on the spot in connection with cash purchases. Later there was an elaborate series of applications, proofs, affidavits, public notices, and other types of documents executed over a period of years in later homestead and mineral entries. Persons making warrant or scrip entries were required to surrender the warrant or scrip they owned to the Register at the time of making entry.

When all requirements of the laws and of the General Land Office had been fulfilled, all papers executed or filed with the Register in the process of such fulfillment (including duplicate record copies of receipts and other documents issued by the register and receiver to the entryman) were forwarded to the General Land Office in Washington. These papers were always accompanied by a document which took varying forms but is now usually called a “final certificate” (in the case of warrant and scrip entries it is called a “certificate of location”). This document was a formal certification made by the Register of the district land office to the Commissioner of the General Land Office that an entryman had fulfilled all legal requirements for obtaining a patent to a described piece of land, and that he was entitled to such patent. The papers were then examined in the General Land Office and, if all was found to be proper, a patent was prepared and sent, usually to the Register of the district office where the entry had been made, for delivery to the entryman. The General Land Office was often so far behind in its work that there was an interval of six months to three years between the receipt of the land-entry papers and the issuance of the patent.

The first district land office was opened at Steubenville, Ohio, on July 2, 1800; the last new land office at Newcastle, Wyoming on March 1, 1920. In the interval, some 362 district land offices were opened. In 1890 there were 123 active offices, the peak number.

The Territory of Dakota was established by an act of March 2, 1861 (12 Stat. 239, 242). William F. Shaffer was confirmed by the Senate as the first U.S. Marshal for the Territory on March 27, 1861. The Territory was divided into North and South Dakata when admitted to the Union as two states on November 2, 1889 (25 Stat. 676, 682).

Both the offices of U.S. marshals and the original court system for the United States were created by the Judiciary Act of September 24, 1789 (1 Stat. 73, 87).  This act contained provisions relative to the operation of the office. Each marshal was given two specific tasks: first, to attend the district and circuit courts and also the U.S. Supreme Court when sitting in his district; and second, to execute throughout his district all lawful precepts directed to him under authority of the United States. He was also empowered to command all necessary assistance in the execution of his duties and to appoint one or more deputies as needed.

Nothing in the Judiciary Act, however, specified who was to exercise the power of  appointment or removal. Nevertheless, President George Washington appointed, and the U.S. Senate confirmed, the initial thirteen U.S. marshals based on the authority of Article II, Section 2 of the Constitution, which provides in pertinent part that the President, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, shall appoint officers who are not enumerated in the Constitution but who are otherwise provided for by “Law”. The Act of February 13, 1801 (2 Stat. 99) is the earliest which gave statutory recognition to the President''s power of appointment or removal, and that recognition has been repeated in subsequent statutes which established new judicial districts and the offices of marshal therein.

In the years following 1789, Congress began to impose upon the marshals such a variety of assignments that they became the “handy-men” of Federal administration. They were directed to take the census (1 Stat. 101) and to hire and supervise jails for Federal prisoners 91 Stat. 225). Marshals were given custody of all vessels and good seized by revenue officers (1 Stat. 275) and became responsible for summoning appraisers to value goods in execution of judgment (1 Stat. 333). Other statutes authorized marshals to sell lands possessed by the United States in satisfaction of judgments (2 Stat. 61); to prosecute all violations of the Act to prevent cruelty to animals while in transit (17 Stat. 485); and to become fiscal agents of the courts (1 Stat. 275), local agents of the comptroller in serving notice upon delinquent officers accountable (1 Stat. 441), and direct agents of the President in executing orders issued by him under the Alien Acts of 1798 (1 Stat. 570, 577).

Not only was the early marshal required to perform a vast number of duties, he was accountable for the performance of those duties to a number of superiors. He reported to the respective courts for which he was really an administrative officer, to the Secretary of the Treasury (3 Stat. 596), and to the Secretary of the Interior (9 Stat. 395). Additionally, he was required to report certain types of suits to the Solicitor of the Treasury (4 Stat. 441) and to furnish statements on prize vessels and cargoes to the Secretary of the Navy (12 Stat. 608). In 1861 the Attorney General was given supervisory powers over marshals (12 Stat. 285), and those powers were reaffirmed in the statute of June 22, 1870, which created the Department of Justice (16 Stat. 162). On November 23, 1956, the Executive Office of U.S. Marshals was established in the Department of Justice to supervise and provide general executive assistance to U.S. marshals and to serve as liaison between them and other divisions of the Department. These functions were taken over by the U.S. Marshals Service (USMS), established in the Department of Justice by DOJ Order 415-69, May 12, 1969.

The current statutory functions of U.S. marshals are set forth in Chapter 37 of Title 28, U.S. Code. Generally, the U.S. marshal in each district attends upon the court and preserves order in the courtroom. He serves all lawful writs and orders issued under authority of the United States. Under service of process he can seize goods and chattels, store seized items, sell property, and sometimes operate businesses under court order. In the District of Columbia U.S. marshals execute eviction notices. He oversees the transportation and commitment of prisoners. Finally, the U.S. marshal in each district pay the official salaries of department of Justice and U.S. court personnel as well as witness and juror fees from appropriated funds.

U.S. district courts have had original jurisdiction in all bankruptcy matters since the passage of the Bankruptcy Act of 1867 (14 Stat. 517), March 2, 1867. Under the provisions of the Bankruptcy Act of 1898 (30 Stat. 544), July 1, 1898, and for the next 80 years, a "bankruptcy court" existed whenever a district court judge, or a group of district court judges, adjudicated a bankruptcy case. Officers of the court known as "bankruptcy referees" performed bankruptcy-related administrative tasks and exercised limited judicial responsibilities.

Although the Bankruptcy Act of 1898 concentrated on debt liquidation, it did introduce provisions for the rehabilitation of distressed businesses. Subsequent legislation, by focusing on reorganization after debt liquidation, resulted in a substantial increase in bankruptcy cases and the vesting of the bankruptcy referees with quasi-judicial powers to facilitate business reorganizations. In a move to modernize the bankruptcy code, Congress passed a joint resolution establishing the Commission on the Bankruptcy Laws of the United States (84 Stat. 468), July 24, 1970. The Commission''s recommendations in its final report of July 30, 1973, formed the basis of the Bankruptcy Reform Act''s provisions.

The Bankruptcy Reform Act (92 Stat. 2549), approved November 6, 1978, left the original jurisdiction of bankruptcy cases with the U.S. district courts, but it established bankruptcy courts "one for each Federal judicial district "and declared them to be "adjuncts to" the regular U.S. district courts. Abolishing the position of bankruptcy referee, the act provided for bankruptcy judges to be appointed by the President for a 14-year term, with Senate confirmation. It also designated the senior active judge under age 70 of each U.S. bankruptcy court as that court''s chief judge, and gave the chief judge the responsibility of dividing the court''s business whenever the rules and orders of the court did not otherwise provide.

The quasi-independent status accorded to the U.S. bankruptcy courts in 1978 by the Bankruptcy Reform Act lasted only until 1982, when the Supreme Court struck down the act''s provisions dealing with the courts and their judges. In Northern Pipeline Construction Co. v. Marathon Pipe Line Co. (458 U.S. 50), the Court declared that the act had in effect created a kind of executive branch ("Article II") court system whose scope and authority ran counter to the provisions of Article III of the Constitution, from which the Federal judicial system derived.

Congress acted to bring the bankruptcy courts into line with the Supreme Court''s ruling by enacting the Bankruptcy Amendments and Federal Judgeship Act of 1984 (98 Stat. 333), July 10, 1984. Like its predecessors, that act left the U.S. district courts with original jurisdiction over bankruptcy cases. The act rescinded the quasi-independence of the bankruptcy court system, however, by declaring the bankruptcy courts to be "units of" the U.S. district courts; by designating bankruptcy court judges as judicial officers of the U.S. district courts; by vesting the appointment of the chief judge of each U.S. bankruptcy court with the district court; and by giving the district court residual authority over the bankruptcy court''s division of its business.

Despite those provisions to reduce the extent of the bankruptcy courts'' independence from the regular district courts, the act left the bankruptcy courts with a great deal of administrative autonomy. Bankruptcy judges are not appointed by the district courts, as they were under the Bankruptcy Act of 1898, but rather by the circuit court of appeals. Under current practice, district courts automatically refer bankruptcy cases to the bankruptcy court. Moreover, primary authority over the division of the bankruptcy courts'' business is in the hands of the bankruptcy courts. The chief judge of each district court appoints the chief judge of the bankruptcy court, but otherwise the district court chief judge has only residual authority to provide by rule for the division of business among bankruptcy judges. In addition, the bankruptcy courts maintain separate clerks from those of the district courts. These clerks manage the bankruptcy courts'' own dockets and cases. The Administrative Office of the United States Courts funds the bankruptcy courts separately from the district courts, and the bankruptcy courts manage their own funds for their operations.

On July 16, 1958, the Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare approved establishment of the Division of General Medical Sciences. On October 17, 1962, Public Law 87-838 authorized the Surgeon General to establish an institute to conduct and support research and research training in the general or basic medical sciences and in related natural or behavioral sciences that have significance for two or more other institutes of NIH, or that lie outside the general areas of responsibility of any other institute.  This became effective on January 30, 1963, when the Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare approved establishment of the National Institute of General Medical Sciences (NIGMS).

The National Institute of General Medical Sciences supported basic biomedical research that laid the foundation for advances in disease diagnosis, treatment, and prevention. The Institute''s training programs helped provide the most critical element of good research: well-prepared scientists. 

Each year, NIGMS-supported scientists made major advances in understanding fundamental life processes. In the course of answering basic research questions, these investigators also increased our knowledge about the mechanisms and pathways involved in certain diseases. Other grantees developed important new tools and techniques, many of which had medical applications. In recognition of the significance of their work, a number of NIGMS grantees received the Nobel Prize and other high scientific honors.

The institute placed great emphasis on the support of individual, investigator-initiated research grants. It funded a limited number of research center grants in selected fields, including structural genomics, trauma and burn research, and the pharmacological sciences. In addition, NIGMS funded several important resources for basic scientists.

In recent years, NIGMS launched initiatives in such cutting-edge areas as structural genomics (the Protein Structure Initiative), pharmacogenetics, collaborative research initiatives (which includes "glue grants"), and the study of complex biological systems. NIGMS also participated in the new NIH Roadmap for Medical Research, a series of far-reaching initiatives that sought to transform the nation''s biomedical research capabilities and speed the movement of research discoveries from the bench to the bedside.

Certain NIGMS training programs addressed areas in which there is a particularly serious need for well-prepared scientists. One of these, the Medical Scientist Training Program, provided investigators who could bridge the gap between basic and clinical research by supporting research training leading to the combined M.D.-Ph.D. degree. Other programs trained scientists to conduct research in the rapidly growing field of biotechnology and at the interface between the fields of chemistry and biology.

The Liaison and Security Offices (LSO) were staffed by two to four officers and four to six enlisted men (depending on the size of the Kreis). It was their function to observe, advise, and report on the manner in which local German authorities discharged their responsibilities and upon all matters affecting the German people. The senior officer in each field office was designated the military government officer (MGO) and was responsible for the supervision of all members of the detachment and their administration and assignment to specific duties involving such matters as public health, public safety, denazification, youth activities, education, housing, constabulary, the Counter Intelligence Corps (CIC), Control Information Division (CID), and the United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration (UNRRA). In addition, the LSO staffs were responsible for the reeducation and democratization of the German people. The reorientation program was created to meet this objective.

The reorientation program consisted of seminars and town hall meetings conducted by military government officers on the Gemeinde (local) level in their individual geographic district. In these meetings the military government officer instructed local officials and citizenry groups in the principles and practices of democracy. In addition, the local citizenry had the opportunity to raise questions and voice complaints concerning military government policies and procedures.

Throughout their existence, the Liaison and Security Offices were faced with compiling an increasing number of reports and surveys for divisions within the Office of Military Government Wuerttemberg-Baden (OMG/WB) without a corresponding increase in personnel. At times, a single officer was responsible for three or more functions simultaneously. Therefore, it was not unusual to find the MGO and the assistant MGO acting in one or more of the following capacities: Public Health Officer, Public Safety Officer, Intelligence Officer, Real Estate Officer, and Special Branch Officer. Later, the LSOs were able to supplement their clerical and investigative staffs with German civilians.

On August 23, 1948, Office of Military Government Wuerttemberg-Baden General Order Number 3 redesignated Field Operations Group as Field Relations Division. Although the name of the division changed, the organization and functions remained the same. Field Relations Division was "delegated command responsibility for all functions and programs assigned to Liaison and Security Offices." In turn, the Liaison and Security Offices were "delegated command responsibility for the execution of policies, functions, and programs" relating to military government.

James Hartness was appointed Federal Food Administrator for Vermont in August 1917. The work was centralized in the main office at Springfield, with an administrator for each of the 14 counties. Early in 1918 Hartness went abroad on other Government business, and John T. Cushing served as Acting Administrator, with headquarters at St. Albans. In May 1918 Frank H. Brooks was appointed Administrator, and the office was moved to Montpelier. After the Armistice the working force was gradually reduced, and the office was transferred to St. Johnsbury, where its activities ceased early in 1919.

Even before the passage of the Food and Fuel Control Act of August 10, 1917, which officially established the United States Food Administration, steps were taken to select some of the State Food Administrators and to set up some of the State organizations. In July 1917, a group of representative leaders came to Washington to confer with Herbert Hoover; within a few weeks over half the Federal Food Administrators had been chosen. Soon after the food control bill became a law, a roster of the Administrators was completed and they received official appointments from the President. In some instances headquarters were established in the State capitals, but in many other cases the central offices were located elsewhere, usually depending upon the place of residence of the Administrator. The headquarters of the divisions of the State offices were sometimes in other cities than those in which the Federal Food Administrators were located.

In setting up the State Food Administrations, already existing machinery could often be used. Following agricultural conferences held in April, the Federal and State Departments of Agriculture, the agricultural colleges, farmers' organizations, and other agencies had taken measures to put into effect the recommendations of the conference for "more perfect organization and coordination of the Nation's agricultural activities." In particular they had promoted the establishment in each State, in connection with the State Councils of Defense, of "as small central division of food production and conservation composed of representatives of the State department of agriculture, the land-grant college, farmers' organizations, and business agencies." Thus by the time the Federal Food Administrators were designated, in many places work with regard to increasing and conserving the food supply was already being performed, either through State or Territorial committees, which were usually attached to the councils of defense or committees of public safety, or by extension workers of the agricultural colleges. In some instances the person in charge of this work became the Federal Food Administrator, and the Federal and State or Territorial organizations either were combined or worked in close cooperation. In at least some cases the administrative offices of the Food Administrations were partly financed with State funds or were staffed by State employees, although funds were ordinarily provided by the Federal Government for the maintenance of offices, the employment of office personnel, transportation, printing, and similar purposes.

After the State Food Administration was set up, as a further step in decentralization, the Federal Food Administrators usually appointed county and often district, city, and town administrators, who were responsible to them. Many of the county administrators were chosen from among the chairmen of the county councils of defense. The organization of this system of country administrations, which was carried out with some variation from State to State, was begun late in 1917 and was completed by July of the following years. Approximately 3,200 county and district administrators received appointments. Some of the local administrations remained largely paper organizations, but others included directors for particular activities and subdivisions comparable to those of the State offices. None of the administrators were paid for his services.

In the conservation work the State Food Administrations enlisted the cooperation of many groups and organizations. In the first phase of the work, that with the women was given most prominence. In house to house canvasses made in the fall of 1917, housewives were asked to pledge themselves to carry out as far as their circumstances would permit the instructions and advice that the Food Administration would give them from time to time. The woman's committees of the State Councils of Defense, working through and with the local women's organizations, did much to organize and direct these food-pledge campaigns, as they did the other aspects of the women's work of the Administrations. In researching and instructing the women in the home with regard to food conservation and utilization, especial reliance was placed on the home economics specialists of the agricultural colleges and the country home demonstration agents of the Department of Agriculture. Were there were no home demonstration agents the country agricultural agents participated in this work. Funds for the expansion of the extension service conducted by the Federal Government in cooperation with the State agricultural colleges had been provided by the Food Production Act of August 10, 1917, and under this act the number of these extension workers was greatly increased. In carrying on the successive conservation campaigns and in brining before the people the recommendations of the Washington office, the State Food Administrations utilized the libraries, schools, churches, fraternal orders, traveling men, civic societies, chambers of commerce, and retail merchants almost as though they were parts of their own organizations. The fact that almost every family was represented in one or more of the social groups that cooperated with the Administrations made them effective channels for disseminating information and gaining support for the measures of food control. Many of the volunteers working for the Food Administration were at the same time performing work for other war agencies, a practice that made for close ties between the local war organizations.

The Administrators followed no uniform plan in setting up their offices, as it was a policy of the Food Administration that the organization should be kept flexible. The subdivisions of the State offices as they finally developed, however, tended to correspond to those of the Washington office, with differences that in part reflected the differences between regions. 

Aside from units concerned with educational and publicity matters, which were among the first to be set up, it usually became necessary for the Administrators to establish various divisions to deal with the work of enforcement and regulation. Some of the divisions, as needed for a specific region, dealt specifically with enforcement, sugar, baking, hotels, restaurants, retail prices, handling of perishable foods, transportation, grain, flour, dairy products, poultry and eggs, livestock and meat, fish, canned and dried foods, potatoes, pinto beans, and cottonseed.

With much of the work connected with the regulation of essential foodstuffs, the State Food Administrations had little to do except to cooperate in the application of the policies determined in Washington. The manufacturers and wholesalers under the system of license control dealt directly with the Washington office, while retailers whose gross sales did not exceed $100,000 a year were not licensed. In the field of enforcement, the State and local administrations were most directly concerned with the special measures adopted for meeting the wheat and sugar situations. The services of State officials such as dairy and food commissioners and their staffs were enlisted for regulatory and inspection work, and agents were sometimes sent out from Washington to assist in investigations. The Washington office urged the Administrators to obtain the voluntary compliance of businessmen and the public with the food regulations and at first advised against the position of penalties, but as it became apparent that firmer measures were necessary, the State and local administrations were permitted to use such means of enforcement as the revocation or suspension of licenses, the issuance of "unfair" or blacklisting orders, the requiring of refunds or contributions to such organizations as the Red Cross, the requisition and forced sale of goods, and the giving of reprimands.

The States Administration Division, headed by John W. Hallowell, served as the buffer between the U.S. Food Administration Headquarters at Washington and the State Food Administrations.

The State Food Administration offices closed in 1919.

The Office of the General Counsel (OGC) was established by an Act of October 15, 1966 (Public Law 89-670; 80 Stat. 931), which also established the Department of Transportation (DOT) that activated on April 1, 1967. The General Counsel was appointed by the President with confirmation by the Senate and was vested with the functions, powers, and duties as set out in chapter 47 of title 10, United States Code, as amended (Uniform Code of Military Justice). As the chief legal officer of the Department, the General Counsel was responsible for legal services, including responsibility for legal aspects and the drafting of legislation, and had final authority on questions of law. The General Counsel was the legal advisor to the Secretary and was responsible for the supervision, coordination and review of the legal work of the lawyers throughout DOT. It was responsible for the Office of Aviation Consumer Protection and Enforcement, and also coordinated the Department's regulatory program, and involvement in legal proceedings before other agencies, as well as various operational and international legal matters.

The Office coordinated the Department's legislative efforts and regulatory program, and provided expert legal guidance and counsel on issues arising from any mode of transportation, including fiscal law and financial assistance, rulemaking and enforcement, litigation in which the Department was a party or had an interest, and various operational and international legal matters. It provided oversight and support to the Chief Counsel Offices of the Department's Operating Administrations (OAs) to ensure a sound decision making process and promoting compliance with all applicable laws. By working together, OGC and the Chief Counsel Offices ensured that the Secretary, Administrators, and other Departmental officers received accurate, timely, and comprehensive legal guidance. A career Deputy General Counsel served as the Department's Designated Agency Ethics Official, Chief Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) Officer, and Dispute Resolution Specialist.

The Office of the Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2 was responsible for the planning and preparation of orders and, to some extent, for operations pertaining to the collection, evaluation, interpretation and distribution of information of the enemy and of our own forces. The Office kept the Commanding General and Staff informed as to the enemy’s situation and the political situation in countries within the boundaries of the command. Specifically, the Office of the Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, was responsible intelligence, which included the collection, evaluation, interpretation, and distribution of information of the enemy and our own forces; maintenance of contact with other intelligence agencies and with intelligence agencies of Allied governments; evaluation and interpretation of information obtained to determine its probable accuracy, significance, and importance; the determination of the need for military maps and surveys, procurement of maps and supervision of map distribution; and coordination with Allied interrogation agencies on examination and interrogation of enemy prisoners of war and members of our forces who had been captured by the enemy or interned in neutral countries. The last was done in coordination with the G-1 Section on personnel data. It was responsible for counter-intelligence and counter-propaganda. This included the regulation of measures to preserve security in coordination with G-1 for military police matters and those relating to civilians; the regulations of dissemination of information to the public in coordination with the G-3 Section for scope of subject matter and with the G-1 Section for morale matters; censorship in coordination with Adjutant General’s Section for postal matters; dissemination of propaganda to the enemy and to civil population of theater in coordination with the Office of War Information (OWI); supervision of the preparation and use of codes and ciphers; the reception of visitors at the headquarters unless this function was delegated in specific cases to aides; supervision of escorting of visitors; supervision of the collection and disposition of enemy documentary propaganda; preparation of measures to refute enemy propaganda among the troops or the civil population within the theater in coordination with OWI; the regulation of activities of news correspondents, photographers, and broadcaster; and advising the Commanding General and Staff on all matters of public relations, including those listed above. The Office was also responsible for the collection and compilation of historical data pertaining to the operation of the command. On August 14, 1942, Major Robert W. McClenahan was announced as the Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2.

In accordance with Headquarters United States Army Forces in the Middle East (HQ USAFIME) General Orders Number 21, dated November 4, 1942, the Services of Supply, U.S.A.F.I.M.E. was established. This order also transferred all HQ USAFIME general and special staff personnel to the Services of Supply, U.S.A.F.I.M.E., except for the personnel of the Adjutant General’s Section. Per Headquarters Services of Supply, U.S.A.F.I.M.E. General Orders Number 3, dated February 24, 1943, the Office of the Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2 was renamed the Office of the Assistant Chief of Staff, which was the head of the Intelligence and Security Division, under Colonel McClenahan. HQ USAFIME General Orders Number 26, dated December 7, 1942, placed Colonel Uzal G. Ent as the Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2 to HQ USAFIME. HQ USAFIME General Orders Number 8, dated January 31, 1943, required that the general and special staff officers of Headquarters Services of Supply, U.S.A.F.I.M.E., also served in the corresponding positions as staff officers of Headquarters U.S. Army Forces in the Middle East, however, it exempted several positions, including the Office of the Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, from serving in both commands and assigned Colonel William H. Crom as the Acting Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2. On April 5, 1943, the Services of Supply, U.S.A.F.I.M.E., was redesignated as the Army Service Forces, U.S.A.F.I.M.E. by HQ USAFIME General Orders Number 20 and on June 5, 1943, it reverted back to the Services of Supply, U.S.A.F.I.M.E. by HQ USAFIME General Orders Number 33. When the Services of Supply, U.S.A.F.I.M.E. was disbanded on September 12, 1943, in accordance with HQ USAFIME General Orders Number 63, all personnel and activities were transferred to HQ USAFIME with corresponding duties and Colonel McClenahan resumed the position of Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2 for USAFIME. When USAFIME was redesignated on March 1, 1945 as the Africa-Middle East Theater, the organization did not change. Other Assistant Chiefs of Staff, G-2 included: Lieutenant Colonel Paul L. E. Hulliwell, Colonel Robert N. Mackin, and Lieutenant Colonel Jack V. Lanterman.

On January 15, 1980, the Air Force Materials Laboratory was inactivated and its functions continued under the Air Force Wright Aeronautical Laboratories (AFWAL) as the Materials Laboratory, per AFSC Special Order G-144, dated September 14, 1979. This changed the Laboratory from being a named Air Force constituted (AFCON) unit to be identified as functional element within the organizational framework of AFWAL. The action was “to further improve the effectiveness of the Laboratories in providing technology for future systems and to permit concentrating critical science and engineering resources on essential Air Force Research and Development activities.”

The Materials Laboratory conducted the entire Air Force Materials Exploratory Development program, the Air Force Manufacturing Technology program and selected Advanced Development and Research programs. The specific goal of the Laboratory was to establish and conduct major integrated programs which will significantly reduce acquisition and ownership costs of Air Force Systems.

Commanders included: Colonel Dana Brabson (Deputy Director (Acting)), January 15, 1980-August 1980; Mr. George P. Peterson, August 1980-June 1985; and Dr. Gary Denman (Acting), June 1985-?.

On December 13, 1990, the Materials Laboratory became the Materials Directorate in the new Wright Laboratory.

sourceNotes: History of the Air Force Materials Laboratory, vol. ii, pt. ii, March 2000: p. 1-5 (The Air Force Materials Laboratory (AFML); Air Force Wright Aeronautical Laboratories (AFWAL); On 1 July 1979, Hq AFSC acted to realign the structural relationship of AFWAL and the four laboratories, which were to be inactivated as named Air Force constituted (AFCON) units. The laboratories were henceforth to be identified as functional elements within the organizational framework of AFWAL. The action was “to further improve the effectiveness of the Laboratories in providing technology for future systems and to permit concentrating critical science and engineering resources on essential Air Force Research and Development activities.” To laboratory employees, the Directive amounted to a total loss of AFML identity. The action, which was made official by AFSC Special Order G-144 of 14 September 1979, was to be effective on 15 January 1980. As stated by AFWAL Commander Colonel J. Nelson, the reorganization was to improve the environment of a loose Federation of Laboratories operating under the constraints of a small staff and as four autonomous laboratories. The AFWAL implementation plan was approved by Hq AFSC on 21 December 1979 (AFWAL History FY 1979). By Special Order G-167, dated 26 October 1982, Hq AFSC relieved the AFWAL from assignment to the Air Force Systems Command and reassigned the Laboratories to the Aeronautical Systems Division (ASD). ASD' s mission enlarged to include aeronautical technology when the AFWAL formally rejoined the division effective 1 November 1982, Authority AFR 26-2, after having been organizationally separate for two decades. In November 1980, the Laboratory of Immunoregulation (LIR) was established to provide a means for applying new knowledge in immunology to the clinical diagnosis and treatment of patients with immunological disorders. It was part of the Intramural Research Program (renamed Division of Intramural Research in 1989). LIR focused on the study of human immunebiology in normal and disease states.

The Laboratory studied the human B cell cycle from the initial activation steps up through and including proliferation and differentiation. In this regard, LIR scientists delineated the mechanism whereby various lymphokines regulate B cell activation, growth, and differentiation. Other major activities included the identification of cell surface receptors for these lymphokines as well as the cloning of lymphokine genes and their receptors. In addition to conducting basic research of human immune responses, the Laboratory scientists, in the clinical research program, investigated the immunopathogenesis and treatment of a variety of immune-mediated diseases.

LIR scientists also studied the acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). Researchers studied the immunopathogenesis of infection with the AIDS retrovirus as well as the immune response to this virus. LIR investigators extrapolated studies on the structure and expression of the AIDS retrovirus genome to these investigations. 

The Laboratory of Immunoregulation studied the elucidation of cellular and molecular mechanisms in the regulation of the human immune system in health and disease, with emphasis on the immunopathogenic mechanisms of the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection and disease progression. Research included studies of cytokines and chemokines in HIV replication; the latent reservoir of HIV-infected cells in AIDS and its implications for antiretroviral therapy; and immunologic approaches to the treatment of HIV infection.

The rational design of strategies aimed at the prevention and treatment of HIV infection depended on delineating how HIV destroys the immune system. LIR investigated a host factors involved in the evolution of HIV disease that indicated HIV pathogenesis was a multifactorial and multiphasic process. Aspects of this process that were under investigation included: regulation of HIV replication by endogenous cytokines and chemokines; regulation of expression of HIV coreceptors; HIV envelope-mediated intracellular signaling events responsible for immune dysfunction; the role of a latent, inducible reservoir of HIV-infected cells in the pathogenesis of HIV disease and its implication for antiretroviral therapy; contribution of HIV-infected T cells, B cells, dendritic cells, monocyte/macrophages, and multipotent progenitor cells to disease pathogenesis; and the role of immunomodulation in immune reconstitution during antiretroviral therapy for HIV infection. LIR researchers conducted clinical trials to determine the safety and efficacy of drugs for the treatment of HIV infection and its complication and the development of methods for immunologic reconstitution in HIV-infected individuals. Their studies of the epidemiology and pathogenesis of HIV infection and other sexually transmitted diseases were both domestic and international.

Major areas of research included: cellular and molecular mechanisms of HIV immunopathogenesis; regulation of the human immune system, particularly the cellular and molecular mechanisms of activation, proliferation, and differentiation of human T- and B-cells; cellular gene expression during activation of human T and B cells; and pathogenesis and treatment of immune-mediated diseases, particularly vasculitic syndromes.

Anthony S. Fauci served as Chief.

Indian Health Service, November 7, 2023 (Indian Health Manual, [part 3, chapter 11 07/15/2013] In 1963, a joint conference of the BIA [Bureau of Indian Affairs] and the DIH [Division of Indian Health] leadership discussed collaborative efforts to combat the community accident mortality problem among Indians. This conference established a plan for the Accident Prevention Program with the Health Education Branch, DIH, in the lead role and several disciplines supporting implementation in the field. The Office of Environmental Health (OEH) was established with two branches, the EHS [Environmental Health Services] and the SFC [Sanitation Facilities Construction]. The OEH was one of the disciplines responsible for field implementation of the Accident Prevention Program. In 1969, the Congress provided funding and positions for the Accident Prevention Program in the Health Education Program. The Accident Prevention Program was formally transferred to the EHS in 1979, when the name was changed to Community Injury Control, and later to Community Injury Prevention.) https://www.ihs.gov/ihm/pc/part-3/p3c11/
